## Week 7: Fairness I: observational

A platform decides who sees a job ad; a government department decides which benefit requests to check for fraud; a risk score flags defendants in one Florida county as likely to be arrested again. For the last, a newsroom reported that, among people who were not arrested again, Black defendants had been flagged almost twice as often as white defendants. The vendor and others replied that the score was equally accurate for both groups, meaning that among people flagged about the same share were arrested again, and the same decile meant about the same rate in both groups. Both readings of the table are correct. The four rates of a classifier and which way each conditions; the three families of statistical fairness criteria; a four-line identity between prevalence, predictive value and the two error rates, and its consequence: when two groups differ in how often the outcome occurs, a classifier with the same positive predictive value in both (neither 0 nor 1) has different error rates in the two. Why people want different criteria, what each choice and each remedy costs, who pays for it, and what no criterion of this kind can show.

**Required reading:** [Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan, Fairness and Machine Learning, chapter 3: Classification](https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf) ("Formalizing classification" through "Varying thresholds and ROC curves", pages 46 to 50; "Statistical non-discrimination criteria" through the end of "Relationships between criteria", pages 54 to 67; "Inherent limitations of observational criteria", pages 71 to 73) · the same book, chapter 4: Relative notions of fairness ("Equality of opportunity" with its three subsections, the narrow, broad and middle views, pages 81 to 85) · skim chapter 3, "Groups in the population" and "No fairness through unawareness" (pages 52 to 54). If time is short, the pages to keep are 54 to 67 and 81 to 85: pages 46 to 50 are the vocabulary of true and false positive rates, risk scores and ROC curves, and pages 71 to 73 can wait until after the lecture.

**Optional:** [Larson, Mattu, Kirchner and Angwin, How We Analyzed the COMPAS Recidivism Algorithm](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-we-analyzed-the-compas-recidivism-algorithm) (ProPublica, 2016) · [Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05807) (ITCS 2017; section 1 through Theorem 1.1, and section 5) · [Chouldechova, Fair prediction with disparate impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00056) (*Big Data*, 2017; sections 1, 2.1 and 2.3) · chapter 3's case study on credit scoring (pages 67 to 71) and chapter notes (pages 73 to 75) · chapter 4, "Connecting statistical and moral notions of fairness" through "The normative underpinnings of error rate parity" (pages 92 to 101)

**Bring to the class:** one rule or score that sorts people into two groups (admit or reject, flag or clear, treat or not), with the two ways it can be wrong and who pays for each.
